mur_har_habayit.resume: The Har HaBayit is the sacred enclosure containing the whole Temple complex: a 500-ama square, girded by a wall. Five gates give access to it. The eastern wall is the only low wall, so that the Kohen who burns the para, standing atop the Mount of Olives, can see over it the opening of the Heikhal at the moment of sprinkling.
cotes: 500 × 500 amot (≈ 240 × 240 m at 0.48 m per ama)
five gates: two Gates of Chulda in the south, Kiponos in the west, Tadi in the north, Shushan in the east
the eastern wall is the only low wall

sources.citation: all the walls there were high, except the eastern wall, because the Kohen who burns the para stands atop the Mount of Olives, aims, and sees the opening of the Heikhal at the moment the blood is sprinkled.
הַר הַבַּיִת וְהוּא הַר הַמּוֹרִיָּה הָיָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת אַמָּה עַל חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת אַמָּה וְהָיָה מֻקָּף חוֹמָה

mur_har_habayit.note: Tour's choice: nothing blocks the line of sight from the Mount of Olives to the entrance of the Heikhal — no column, no closed gate, no crowd on the east-west axis.

sol_har_habayit.resume: The Temple complex is not set at the center of the mountain: the largest open space is to the south, then to the east, then to the north, the smallest to the west. One enters by the right and exits by the left, except someone to whom something has happened — a mourner, an excommunicate —, who goes around by the left.
cotes: largest open space in the south, then east, then north, smallest in the west

sources.citation: חוּץ מִמִּי שֶׁאֵרְעוֹ דָבָר, שֶׁהוּא מַקִּיף לִשְׂמֹאל
הָעֲזָרָה לֹא הָיְתָה מְכֻוֶּנֶת בְּאֶמְצַע הַר הַבַּיִת

sol_har_habayit.note: Tour's choice: the material of the esplanade's ground, which no source gives.

soreg.resume: The Soreg is a wooden lattice fence that surrounds the whole complex inside the Har HaBayit. Only ten tefachim high, it marks a light separation: it is a barrier, not a wall.
cotes: 10 tefachim high (≈ 0.8 m)

sources.citation: לִפְנִים מִמֶּנּוּ, סוֹרֵג, גָּבוֹהַּ עֲשָׂרָה טְפָחִים
מְחִצָּה הָעֲשׂוּיָה נְקָבִים נְקָבִים כְּמִטָּה מְסֹרֶגֶת בַּחֲבָלִים, וְהִיא עֲשׂוּיָה מַדְּפֵי עֵץ אֲרֻכִּים וּקְצָרִים שֶׁמַּרְכִּיבִין אוֹתָן זוֹ עַל זוֹ בַּאֲלַכְסוֹן

heil.resume: The Cheil is the ten-ama strip that runs between the Soreg and the wall of the Ezrat Nashim. Twelve steps cross it, each half an ama high and half an ama deep.
cotes: 10-ama strip between the Soreg and the wall of the Ezrat Nashim
12 steps
each step: ½ ama high × ½ ama deep

sources.citation: לִפְנִים מִמֶּנּוּ, הַחֵיל, עֶשֶׂר אַמּוֹת. וּשְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה מַעֲלוֹת הָיוּ שָׁם
מֵאוֹתוֹ סוֹרֵג הָיָה מָקוֹם פָּנוּי עֶשֶׂר אַמּוֹת, וְהוּא נִקְרָא חֵיל

heil.note: Adopted: a strip ten amot wide, as Bartenura reads it (Middot 2:3). Set aside: the text of the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:3), which reads « הַחֵיל [גָּבְהוֹ] עֶשֶׂר אַמּוֹת », a height; the word is in brackets, a textual variant. Tour's choice: the ten amot of the Cheil are measured from the projecting gatehouses of the Azara, the outermost part of the wall. Measured from the wall itself, the Soreg would cut through those gatehouses.

portiques.resume: Covered porticoes line the Har HaBayit on all four sides. “The Har HaBayit was a double stav… a stav within a stav” (Pesachim 13b), which Rashi explains: one colonnade runs all around, and inside that circuit another. The model therefore sets two rows of columns along each wall. The same page speaks of the “roof of the itztaba”, on which the two loaves were placed; Rashi specifies that this roof was built against the rain, and the Rambam says the whole Har HaBayit was covered (Beit HaBechirah 5:1). The number of columns, their spacing, profile and height are choices.

portiques.note: Tour's choice: no column stands in front of the five gates of the Har HaBayit or on the east-west axis, to keep clear the view that the low east wall is there to allow (Middot 2:4).

ezrat_nashim.resume: The Court of the Women is the large court east of the Azara. It measures 135 amot on each side, and four roofless chambers occupy its corners.
cotes: open to the sky (tour's choice)
four roofless corner chambers of 40 × 40 amot

sources.citation: וְלִפְנֵי הָעֲזָרָה בַּמִּזְרָח הָיְתָה עֶזְרַת הַנָּשִׁים

ezrat_nashim.note: Tour's choice: the court is shown open to the sky. Middot 2:5 says only of the four corner chambers that they are roofless, « וְלֹא הָיוּ מְקוֹרוֹת ».

porte_est_ezrat_nashim.nom: Eastern Gate of the Ezrat Nashim
porte_est_ezrat_nashim.resume: The Ezrat Nashim is entered from the east: one comes in through the eastern gate of the Har HaBayit, crosses the Cheil and climbs its twelve steps. Sukkah 5:4 calls this gate “the gate that goes out to the east”. To the west, the Gate of Nikanor opens onto the Ezrat Israel; the gates of the Har HaBayit, the Ezrat Nashim and the Azara, and the entrance of the Heikhal, are aligned.
porte_est_ezrat_nashim.note: Adopted: the Gate of Nikanor is the eastern gate of the Azara, which the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:5) also calls Sha'ar HaElyon. Middot 2:6, however, lists a Sha'ar HaElyon among the southern gates; Tosfot Yom Tov (Middot 2:6) reports that the Yerushalmi applies the name to the eastern gate, but holds that the one in Middot 2:6 is in the south.

gezuztra.resume: A gallery ran all around the Ezrat Nashim. It was added for Simchat Beit HaShoeva: the women looked on from above and the men from below, “so that they would not mingle”.
cotes: all around the court, open to the west toward Nikanor, cut at the eastern gate
at the crest of the corner chambers, 15.6 amot above the court
3.5 amot wide

gezuztra.note: No source gives its height: the tour sets it at the crest of the corner chambers, running along their walls on the court side without covering them — they remain roofless (Middot 2:5). Columns, balustrade and frieze are choices. No source says how one went up to it: the tour shows no stair. Set aside: Rashi (Sukkah 51b), for whom corbels stayed in the walls and a floor of planks was laid on them every year. Tour's choice: the gallery is shown empty, even on the night of Simchat Beit HaShoeva; no source says what became of it the rest of the year.

lishkat_haetzim.resume: Northeast corner chamber of the Ezrat Nashim, roofless, forty amot on each side. Wood is sorted here, and Kohanim unfit for service work here. Not to be confused with the Lishkat HaEtz, on the north side of the Azara according to Yoma 19a and the Rambam (the standard text of Middot 5:4 places it in the south).
cotes: 40 × 40 amot, roofless
northeast corner of the Ezrat Nashim

lishkat_hanezirim.resume: Southeast corner chamber of the Ezrat Nashim, roofless, forty amot on each side. The nazirites cook their offerings here.

southeast corner of the Ezrat Nashim

lishkat_beit_shemanya.resume: Southwest corner chamber of the Ezrat Nashim, roofless, forty amot on each side. According to Abba Shaul, it is the storeroom for oil and wine.
cotes: 40 × 40 amot, roofless
southwest corner of the Ezrat Nashim

lishkat_beit_shemanya.note: Adopted: Abba Shaul (Middot 2:5), followed by the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:8). Set aside: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov, who says « שָׁכַחְתִּי מֶה הָיְתָה מְשַׁמֶּשֶׁת », I have forgotten what it was used for.

quinze_marches.resume: Fifteen semicircular steps rise from the Ezrat Nashim to the Ezrat Israel. They correspond to the fifteen Shir HaMaalot of Psalms, and the Leviim stand on them with their instruments to sing during Simchat Beit HaShoeva. Beneath the Ezrat Israel, opening onto the Ezrat Nashim, are the chambers where they stored their instruments, the Lishkot HaLeviim, one on each side of the steps.
cotes: 15 semicircular steps

two chambers, one on each side of the fifteen steps
doors of 3 × 6 amot

lishkot_haleviim.note: What the Mishnah says: chambers beneath the Ezrat Yisrael, opening onto the Ezrat Nashim, where the Levites put down their instruments; neither how many nor where. Tour's choice: two chambers, one on each side of the steps, with doors of 3 × 6 amot — the size in Middot 2:3, twenty by ten, is that of the gates of the Azara, and these chambers are only six and a half amot high —, the cedar shelves, the hooks and where each instrument sits. No chatzotzrot: the mishnah does not name them among what is put down there, and the kohanim blow them (Numbers 10:8). At Simchat Beit HaShoevah, however, the Levites play them on the fifteen steps (Sukkah 5:4). Modeled: two chambers of 10.5 × 6 amot under the paving of the Ezrat Yisrael.

lishkat_hakelim.resume: Whoever wished to donate a vessel to the Temple threw it into this chamber. Once every thirty days the treasurers opened it: whatever could serve the upkeep of the Temple was kept, the rest was sold, and the money went to the chamber of the Temple's upkeep.
cotes: beneath the Ezrat Yisrael, to the north, beyond the Levites
door shut, an opening above it to throw in the gifts

lishkat_hakelim.note: No source places this chamber or the Chamber of Secret Gifts: the Raavad wonders at it, quoted by Melekhet Shlomo (Tamid 3:5), and Mishnat Eretz Yisrael suggests that they too opened onto the Ezrat Nashim. The tour places them beneath the Ezrat Yisrael, with the Levites' chambers: a choice. Also a choice: the shut bronze door, the opening for throwing in the gift, the heap of vessels. One does not enter: it was opened only once a month.

lishkat_chashaim.resume: The chamber of discreet gifts. Those who feared sin put money in it in secret, and poor people of good family drew their living from it, in secret too. The Rambam gives it as the example of the gift where the giver does not know to whom he gives, nor the poor man from whom he receives.
cotes: beneath the Ezrat Yisrael, to the south, beyond the Levites
open door, a chest in the middle

The tour places it beneath the Ezrat Yisrael: a choice, as is the cedar chest bound in bronze. Variant: the Sifrei (Devarim 117), quoting the Mishnah, reads “in Jerusalem” instead of “in the Mikdash”; it places nothing in the Temple.

beit_din_har_habayit.nom: Court at the gate of the Har HaBayit
beit_din_har_habayit.translit: Beit din she'al petach Har HaBayit
beit_din_har_habayit.resume: The first of Jerusalem's three courts, a court of twenty-three. A sage whose teaching was disputed in his town came here first; if the judges had a tradition, they said it, otherwise one went up to the court at the gate of the Azara, then to the Great Sanhedrin in the Lishkat HaGazit. Tiferet Yisrael places it just inside the eastern gate of the Har HaBayit, the one topped by the image of Shushan HaBirah: it sits under the portico, beside the passage of the gate. The judges sit in a half-circle, the wisest in the middle so that he sees them all; two scribes stand before them, and three rows of students sit facing them.
cotes: 23 judges in a half-circle, the wisest in the middle
two scribes standing
three rows of students, the first the closest

beit_din_har_habayit.note: What the texts say: three courts (Sanhedrin 11:2), two of them of twenty-three; Tiferet Yisrael puts this one “inside the eastern gate of the wall of the Har HaBayit”, and Haggahot Ya'avetz names that gate: the one bearing Shushan HaBirah. The Tosefta (Sanhedrin 7:1) says only “one on the Har HaBayit”. The half-circle, the scribes and the students hold for a court of twenty-three as for the great one (Tosafot Yom Tov on Sanhedrin 4:3, citing Rashi). Tour's choice: the south side of the gate, under the double portico (Pesachim 13b), between the wall and the first row of columns; the two tiers and the seats. The Rambam counts twenty-three students per row (Sanhedrin 1:7): the scene shows the three rows, not every student, and reads « לְמַטָּה הֵימֶנָּה » as “further away”. Set aside: Rashi (Sanhedrin 86b) and Bartenura, who put it at the eastern gate of the Ezrat Nashim; the Tosefta, which gives it only three judges.

beit_din_haazara.nom: Court at the gate of the Azara
beit_din_haazara.resume: The second of Jerusalem's three courts, a court of twenty-three. One went up to it when the court at the gate of the Har HaBayit had no tradition on the question; if it had none either, one went to the Great Sanhedrin in the Lishkat HaGazit. Tiferet Yisrael places it just inside the eastern gate of the Ezrat Nashim: the judges sit with their backs to the colonnade of the gallery, facing the Nikanor gate.
cotes: 23 judges in a half-circle, the wisest in the middle
two scribes standing
three rows of students, the first the closest

beit_din_haazara.note: What the texts say: three courts (Sanhedrin 11:2), two of them of twenty-three; Tiferet Yisrael puts this one “inside the eastern gate of the Ezrat Nashim”. The half-circle, the scribes and the students hold for a court of twenty-three as for the great one (Tosafot Yom Tov on Sanhedrin 4:3, citing Rashi). Tour's choice: the south side of the gate, backed onto the colonnade of the gallery, with a passage left in front of the shofarot; the two tiers and the seats. The Rambam counts twenty-three students per row (Sanhedrin 1:7): the scene shows the three rows, not every student. Set aside: Rashi (Sanhedrin 86b), who puts it at the end of the Ezrat Nashim, before the Ezrat Yisrael; the Tosefta (Sanhedrin 7:1), which puts it “in the Cheil”, whose ten amot the twelve steps already take, and gives it only three judges.

shaar_nikanor.resume: The Gate of Nikanor opens the Azara to the east, at the top of the fifteen steps. It is the only gate of the Azara left in bronze when the others were plated with gold, in memory of the miracle of the gates that came from Alexandria; others say it was because its bronze shone like gold. According to Abba Yossi ben Chanan, two small side gates (pishpeshin) flank it.
cotes: 20 amot high × 10 wide (standard dimension of the gates of the Azara)
two side pishpeshin, according to Abba Yossi ben Chanan (Middot 2:6)
bronze, against the gold of the other gates

shaar_nikanor.note: Tour's choice: the gate is shown open, its leaves folded back into the gateway, as during the service; Sukkah 5:5 speaks only of trumpet blasts “for the opening of the gates”, without saying how long they stayed open. Closed, it would cut the line of sight that the low east wall is there to allow. The pishpeshin come from the list of thirteen gates of Abba Yossi ben Chanan (Middot 2:6); Middot 1:4 gives Nikanor two lishkot, those of Pinchas HaMalbish and of the Osei Chavitin. Set aside: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov (Yoma 38a), for whom it was a polished bronze, « נְחֹשֶׁת קְלוֹנִיתָא », that shone like gold.

azara.resume: The Azara is the inner court, where the service is performed. It measures 187 amot east to west and 135 north to south. From east to west it is divided into the Ezrat Israel, the Ezrat Kohanim, the Mizbeach, the space between the altar and the Ulam, the Building, then the rear of the Kodesh HaKodashim. The floor is laid in rows of stone slabs; the Kohanim serve there barefoot.
cotes: 187 amot (east-west) × 135 amot (north-south) ≈ 90 × 65 m
east → west: Ezrat Israel 11, Ezrat Kohanim 11, Mizbeach 32, between altar and Ulam 22, Building 100, rear of Kodesh HaKodashim 11
north → south: 8, Beit HaMitbachayim 12.5, marble tables 8, rings 24, rings → altar 8, Mizbeach 32, Kevesh 30, ramp → south wall 12.5

לְהִתְחַמֵּם שָׁם הַכֹּהֲנִים מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהוֹלְכִים יְחֵפִים

azara.note: Adopted: the Rambam's division (Beit HaBechirah 5:13–15). From north to south, Middot 5:2 leaves 25 amot without figures — between the ramp and the wall on one side, for the pillars on the other; the Rambam gives 12.5 to each. He also reorders the north side: Middot 5:2 counts rings → tables 4, tables → pillars 4, pillars → wall 8, the Rambam wall → Beit HaMitbachayim 8, Beit HaMitbachayim 12.5, tables 8.

portes_azara.nom: North and South Gates of the Azara
portes_azara.resume: Seven gates pierce the wall of the Azara: three in the south, three in the north, and Nikanor in the east. They measure twenty amot high by ten wide. They are counted starting from the westernmost: in the south, Sha'ar HaDelek, Sha'ar HaBekhorot, then Sha'ar HaMayim, the easternmost; in the north, Sha'ar HaNitzotz, Sha'ar HaKorban, then Beit HaMoked.
cotes: 7 gates: 3 in the south, 1 in the east, 3 in the north
20 amot high × 10 wide
three gate structures 20 amot wide, projecting 12 amot beyond the wall (tour's choice, without source)

שְׁעָרִים דְּרוֹמִיִּים סְמוּכִים לַמַּעֲרָב, שַׁעַר הָעֶלְיוֹן, שַׁעַר הַדֶּלֶק, שַׁעַר הַבְּכוֹרוֹת, שַׁעַר הַמָּיִם

portes_azara.note: Adopted: seven gates, following Middot 1:4–5. Set aside: the thirteen gates of Abba Yossi ben Chanan (Middot 2:6, Shekalim 6:3); yet it is his list that gives the direction of counting, « סְמוּכִים לַמַּעֲרָב », which the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:4) repeats without the names, while Middot 1:4–5 gives none. The southern names are in Middot 1:4, the northern ones in Middot 1:5; Yoma 19a reads Sha'ar HaDelaka and Sha'ar HaKorban in the south, without changing the place of Sha'ar HaMayim, and Sha'ar Beit HaMoked in the north. Tour's choice: the spacing of the gates, which no source gives, and the 20 × 12 amot gate structure with its twenty steps, which have no source.

doukhan.resume: The Dukhan is the platform of the Leviim, set at the boundary between the Ezrat Israel and the Ezrat Kohanim, according to R. Eliezer ben Yaakov (Middot 2:6) on the one-ama step that separates the two courts, with three half-ama steps. The Leviim stand on it to sing, with their instruments. Never fewer than twelve are counted, and any number may be added beyond that. The Levite children, according to R. Eliezer ben Yaakov (Arakhin 2:6), stand below, their heads between the legs of the Leviim.

set on the one-ama step that separates the Ezrat Israel and the Ezrat Kohanim
never fewer than twelve Leviim standing
at least nine kinorot, two to six nevalim, a single tziltzal

doukhan.note: Adopted: the view of R. Eliezer ben Yaakov (Middot 2:6) — a one-ama step separates the Ezrat Israel from the Ezrat Kohanim, and the Dukhan stands on it. According to the first view in the mishna, the two courts are separated only by a row of projections (rashei pispasin).

ezrat_israel.resume: Two strips of eleven amot each, east of the Azara: the Ezrat Israel, where the people stand, then the Ezrat Kohanim to the west. According to the first view in the mishna, projections, rashei pispasin, separate them; according to R. Eliezer ben Yaakov, it is a one-ama step, and this is where the Dukhan stands. The people do not cross into the Ezrat Kohanim, except for the semikha, the shechita and the tenufa.
cotes: Ezrat Israel: 11 amot out of the 187 east to west
Ezrat Kohanim: the next 11 amot to the west
135 amot wide
one-ama step between the two, according to R. Eliezer ben Yaakov

וְרָאשֵׁי פִסְפָּסִין מַבְדִּילִין בֵּין עֶזְרַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְעֶזְרַת הַכֹּהֲנִים. רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר, מַעֲלָה הָיְתָה שָׁם, וּגְבוֹהָה אַמָּה, וְהַדּוּכָן נָתוּן עָלֶיהָ

ezrat_israel.note: Adopted: a one-ama step between the Ezrat Israel and the Ezrat Kohanim, carrying the Dukhan, following R. Eliezer ben Yaakov (Middot 2:6). Set aside: the mere row of projections (rashei pispasin) of the first view in the mishna.

mizbeach.resume: The outer altar, built of stones untouched by iron, joined with plaster and whitewashed with lime twice a year. Its base, the yessod, is 32 amot on each side and one ama high; a one-ama setback gives 30 × 30 up to the sovev, the walkable ledge at six amot; a second setback gives 28 × 28 up to the surface of the fire. Four hollow horns, one ama by one ama, occupy the corners. It is not centered on the axis of the Heikhal: it is offset nine amot to the south.
cotes: yessod: 32 × 32 amot, 1 ama high
30 × 30 up to the sovev, at 6 amot high (1 yessod + 5)
28 × 28 up to the surface (ma'arakha)

mizbeach.note: Adopted: the altar shifted to the south, its center nine amot south of the axis of the Heikhal. This is what the measurements of Middot 5:2 give as the Rambam reads them, and the view of R. Eliezer ben Yaakov, who wants the “north” — where the most holy offerings are slaughtered — free of everything, even of the altar (Zevachim 59a). Set aside: R. Yehuda's altar centered in front of the Heikhal (Zevachim 58b), which many models follow, and R. Yosei HaGelili's altar lying entirely in the north (Zevachim 59a). The round figures are those of the first opinion in Middot 3:1, where R. Yosei describes an original altar of 28 × 28 that the returning exiles enlarged by four amot to the south and west; the Rambam counts in tefachim (Beit HaBe'hira 2:7): a yessod of five tefachim, a surface of 28 amot and four tefachim, a ma'arakha of 24 amot and four tefachim. Choice of the tour: the height of ten amot, as nine to the surface plus one for the horn, which the Rambam does not give in this way.

kevesh.resume: The ramp that rises to the altar, to the south, in its extension. 32 amot long and 16 wide, it starts from the ground and reaches the surface, its last two amot overhanging the yessod and the sovev, with a little air between it and the altar. Two small ramps branch off from it: to the east toward the sovev, to the west toward the yessod. In its west face is the revuva, a one-ama niche where disqualified bird chatat offerings were placed; to the west stand two tables, of marble for the limbs and of silver for the vessels; to the east, on the floor, the heap where the terumat hadeshen is set down. The altar has no staircase: the Torah forbids it.

shit.note: Adopted: the shit is the cavity beneath the altar into which the wine and water of the libations flow, as Bartenura and the Rambam read it in their commentaries on Middot 3:3. Set aside: the Tiferet Yisrael, for whom it is the cavity into which the blood drains. Not shown: the two blood holes and the channel that carries the blood away (Middot 3:2). maarakhot.resume: The woodpiles set up on the surface of the altar. According to R. Yosei, three fires burn there, and four on Yom Kippur. In the center is the tapuach, the mound of ash that the logs of the great ma'arakha touch. Among the miracles of the Temple, the Mishnah counts that the rain did not put out the fire of the ma'arakha and the wind did not prevail over the column of smoke.

lishkat_hagazit.resume: Seat of the Sanhedrin, and place where the lots for the Kohanim were drawn. It straddles the north wall of the Azara, half within the sacred area, half outside it: the wall breaks off across its width, and the boundary is marked on the floor. Two openings, one onto the Azara in the south, the other onto the chol in the east, at the top of twenty steps coming up from the terrace of the Cheil. The Gemara calls them petachim, not sha'arim — they are not gates of the Azara. Its walls are of hewn stone broken by courses of cedar; in the chol half, where the court sits, the floor is of cedar and the far wall is lined with carved cedar panels. In the sacred half, the Kohanim stand in a circle for the drawing of lots, and they come there to read the Shema. The Sanhedrin sits in the chol half, since no one sits in the Azara except the kings of the house of David. It sits in a semicircle, so that the judges see one another: the Nasi in the middle, the Av Beit Din at his right, two scribes standing before them — three according to R. Yehuda —, and three rows of students seated facing the judges. It sits there from the morning Tamid until the evening one; on Shabbat and festivals, it sits on the Cheil. There it judges the Kohanim: one found unfit dresses in black and leaves, one found fit dresses in white and goes in to serve with his brothers. Two courts of twenty-three sit below, at the eastern gates of the Har HaBayit and of the Ezrat Nashim: one goes up from one to the other, then here (Sanhedrin 11:2).

lishkat_hagazit.note: Adopted: the distribution of Yoma 19a and the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:17) — Melach, Parva and Medichin in the south, Etz, Gola and Gazit in the north. The standard text of Middot 5:3–4 reverses the two sides; Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 5:3) notes the variant. The Rambam also places these chambers “in the Ezrat Israel”; the tour sets them against the wall of the Azara. Set aside: the orientation of the baraita in Yoma 25a, “the lottery in its east, and the elder sitting in its west,” from which Abaye infers that the sacred half is to the east and the non-sacred half to the west; straddling the north wall, the tour's room has its sacred half to the south and its non-sacred half to the north. Also set aside: R. Yehuda, for whom the scribes are three (Sanhedrin 4:3). Tour's choice: the opening onto the non-sacred area to the east, and its twenty steps — Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 5:4) says one went up to it by steps, without giving their number; the decoration, which the Gemara only calls "like a great basilica", taken from the Tanakh and not from Roman architecture: courses of cedar beams in the stone as in the walls of Solomon's court, a cedar floor like his hall of judgment, a far wall of framed cedar panels whose rails carry the gourds and flowers of the Bayit, a ceiling of cedar beams; the three tiers and the Nasi's dais; seats modelled on Solomon's throne, with a rounded back and armrests but without its lions, the Nasi's overlaid with gold; the scribes' lecterns and the students' benches; the boundary marked on the floor, by analogy with the Beit HaMoked, of which Middot 1:6 says it. The room shows the layout of the court, not its numbers: seventy-one judges and three rows of students do not fit in it.

Second of the three chambers of the north, inside the courtyard against the wall, west of the Lishkat HaGazit and in front of the Lishkat HaEtz; the roof of the three is at the same level.

lishkat_haetz.note: Adopted: the distribution of Yoma 19a and the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:17) — Melach, Parva and Medichin in the south, Etz, Gola and Gazit in the north. The standard text of Middot 5:3–4 reverses the two sides; Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 5:3) notes the variant. The Rambam also places these chambers “in the Ezrat Israel”; the tour sets them against the wall of the Azara. Also adopted: the arrangement Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 5:4) draws from “behind the two of them” — HaGazit in front, to the east; HaGola behind it, on the courtyard side; HaEtz behind HaGola, its back to the north, hence on the far side of the wall, on the terrace of the Cheil. The standard text of Middot 5:3–4 reverses the two sides; Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 5:3) notes the variant. Tour's choice: the ma'ake of the bath, the hides stacked on a bench and the heap of salt. Not shown: the linen sheet and the steps of the bath.

The standard text of Middot 5:3–4 reverses the two sides; Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 5:3) notes the variant. The Rambam also places these chambers “in the Ezrat Israel”; the tour sets them against the wall of the Azara. Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 5:3) gives this chamber two openings onto the Azara: one for the work, the other at the foot of the stairway, so that the Kohen Gadol goes up to the bath without passing where the entrails are rinsed; the tour follows this layout, the entrance of the stairway being the second. Not shown: the partition he places along the stairway, so that whoever goes up does not see into the chamber. Tour's choice: the round shape of the stairway (mesiba means “spiral”), the trough and the two marble tables.

beit_hamoked.resume: The large house where the Kohanim on duty sleep, on the north wall of the Azara: it is the third gate of the north counted by Middot 1:5, the easternmost in the tour. It straddles the wall, which breaks off across its width: a large hall at the level of the Azara, its door to the sacred area in the south, the one to the Cheil in the north, at the top of twenty steps. Four small chambers open onto the hall, two in the sacred area, two outside, a marble strip (rashei pispasin) marking the boundary: the lambs for the korban, the showbread, the altar stones hidden by the Hasmoneans, and the descent to the ritual bath. Along the walls, the stone tiers where the elders sleep.

beit_hamoked.note: Adopted: straddling the boundary of the sacred area — two of its chambers “in the sacred area” and two “outside” (Middot 1:6), the building “partly within the Azara” according to Bartenura. Set aside: the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:9), who puts it “on the north of the Azara, outside, between the Azara and the Cheil”; and the kippa of Middot 1:8, a vault for Bartenura (“כִּפָּה ארקוול"ט”) as for the Rambam (“וְהָיָה בָּנוּי כִּפָּה”) — the tour shows none. Tour's choice: the order of the gates counted from the west, the view of Abba Yossi ben Chanan (Middot 2:6) taken up by the Rambam (5:4), and their even spacing, which puts the Beit HaMoked near the north-east corner; the hall at the level of the Azara, the size of the four small chambers, the placement of the twenty steps and the furnishings.

mesiba_bira.resume: The underground passage of the kohen on watch who became impure during the night. From the north-west chamber of the Beit HaMoked, a spiral of steps sinks beneath the Azara; a tunnel lit by lamps on both sides leads to the Beit HaTevila. The bira is the whole Mikdach, and the mesiba runs beneath it. It is not sanctified — a tunnel opening onto the Har HaBayit is not — which is why the impure kohen may walk through it.

There is a fire there and a "privy of honor": found locked, one knows someone is inside.

shaar_hamayim.resume: The easternmost of the gates of the south wall of the Azara — three according to Middot 1:4, four according to Abba Yossi ben Chanan (Middot 2:6). According to the Jerusalem Talmud (Yoma 1:5), the Lishkat Beit Avtinas is built above it; Yoma 19a places there the first immersion of the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur. The tour sets the Lishkat Parhedrin against it to the west. Its gate structure is hollow: twenty steps rise inside it from the terrace of the Cheil up to the level of the Azara.

Its position, the easternmost, follows the order “near the west” of Abba Yossi ben Chanan (Middot 2:6; Shekalim 6:3), taken up by the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:4); placing the Lishkat Parhedrin west of the gate is also a choice.

beit_avtinas.resume: The chamber of the Avtinas family, where the incense is prepared. According to the Jerusalem Talmud, it is built above Sha'ar HaMayim: the tour sets it as an upper floor on that gate, at the east end of the south wall, against the Lishkat Parhedrin. The Kohen Gadol is brought there on the eve of Kippur. His first immersion of the day takes place close by, “on top of Sha'ar HaMayim, beside his chamber” (Yoma 19a), not in the Avtinas chamber. Inside, the mortar in which the incense is pounded, the makhteshet — the one from Beit Avtinas is counted, along with the Table and the Menora, among what was carried off to Rome —, and the table where the eleven sammanim are weighed before each is pounded separately. The Avtinas family kept the secret of the incense, and the Mishna counts it to their shame. The Sages dismissed them and brought craftsmen from Alexandria: these knew how to blend the spices, but not how to make the smoke rise — theirs spread out every which way, while that of the Avtinas rose straight as a stick. When recalled, the family came back only for doubled wages. Their reason: they knew the Temple was destined to be destroyed, and feared that an unworthy man would learn the craft and use it for idolatry. They are praised as well: no bride ever went out perfumed from their homes, so that no one would say they perfumed themselves with the incense. After the destruction, one of them handed Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri the scroll of spices, and Rabbi Akiva said: from now on, it is forbidden to speak ill of them.

beit_avtinas.note: Adopted: the Jerusalem Talmud (Yoma 1:5), the only source to put the Avtinas chamber “above Sha'ar HaMayim”; the tour takes it literally and makes it an upper story (Tamid 1:1) built on top of the gatehouse. Open question: Yoma 19a gives the Kohen Gadol two chambers, Parhedrin and Avtinas, one in the north and one in the south, without knowing which is where; its reasoning would put Avtinas in the north before being rejected, and Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 5:4) also considers Avtinas in the north. By putting both Avtinas and Parhedrin in the south, the tour departs from Yoma 19a. Tour's choice: the one-ama walls, the 3 × 4 window onto the Azara, the table, the scale and the bowls, since the sources name only the mortar. No source says what the mortar was made of; the tour makes it bronze, as the Rambam requires the vessels of the service to be of metal (Beit HaBechirah 1:18).

shaar_hanitzotz.resume: The westernmost of the three gates of the north wall of the Azara. It carries the chamber of the Beit HaNitzotz on its upper floor. Its gate structure is hollow: twenty steps rise inside it from the terrace of the Cheil up to the level of the Azara.

shaar_hanitzotz.note: Tour's choice: the gate structure of 20 × 12 amot and its twenty steps have no source — nothing says where one climbs from the terrace of the Cheil to the level of the Azara. Middot 2:6, where Abba Yossi ben Chanan calls the north gates “near the west,” does not name Sha'ar HaNitzotz: the tour makes it the westernmost by reading the order of Middot 1:5 (Nitzotz, Korban, Beit HaMoked) from west to east. The sources give this order, not the spacing: the gates are spread evenly.

beit_hanitzotz.resume: The chamber built as an upper floor (aliyah) above Sha'ar HaNitzotz, on the north wall of the Azara, where the kohanim keep watch. Middot 1:5 describes this aliyah without naming it; Tamid 1:1 counts the Beit HaNitzotz among the watch posts of the kohanim and makes it an aliyah: the tour identifies the two.

lishkat_parhedrin.note: Open question: Yoma 19a gives the Kohen Gadol two chambers, Parhedrin and Avtinas, one in the north and one in the south, “and we do not know” which is where; the Gemara finds Parhedrin in the south more plausible, then rejects the argument. Only the Jerusalem Talmud (Yoma 1:5) puts the Avtinas chamber “above Sha'ar HaMayim, and next to his chamber”: the tour sets the Lishkat Parhedrin against it, and so puts both chambers in the south, which Yoma 19a rules out. Set aside: Bartenura (Middot 5:4) and the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:17) identify the Lishkat Parhedrin with the Lishkat HaEtz — in the north according to the Rambam, in the south in the text of the Mishna that Bartenura comments on — which Abba Shaul says was the chamber of the Kohen Gadol (Middot 5:4). Tour's choice: its place west of the gate.

lishkat_osei_chavitin.resume: One of the two chambers flanking the Gate of Nikanor, in the Ezrat Israel according to the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:17) — the other being the Lishkat Pinchas HaMalbish. The chavitin are made here, the daily offering of the Kohen Gadol, kneaded, shaped and baked within the sacred enclosure: a table, a hearth, and the pan, the machavat of Leviticus 6:14, flat according to R. Chananya ben Gamliel.

Tour's choice: the arrangement of the table, hearth and pan.

lishkat_pinchas.resume: One of the two chambers flanking the Gate of Nikanor, in the Ezrat Israel according to the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:17) — the other being the Lishkat Osei Chavitin. Pinchas is in charge of the Kohanim's vestments: along the walls, closed cupboards where each watch stores its own.

Tour's choice: the Rambam does not say where the ninety-six garment cabinets were, four per watch (Klei HaMikdash 8:8); the tour places them here, with the man in charge of the garments, in six rows.

portes_houlda.resume: The two gates of the south, “used for entering and exiting”: it is through them that the people go up to the Har HaBayit and come back down. The Mishna does not say where they open in the wall. Middot 2:3 gives the gates a height of 20 amot and a width of 10, and the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 5:2) says so explicitly of the gates of the Har HaBayit. Like every gate of the Temple except Tadi, they are capped with a lintel, not an arch. The tour sets a timora on each of their jambs, taken from Ezekiel.

portes_houlda.note: Tour's choice: the timorot on the jambs come from Ezekiel 40:26, which describes the future Temple; Middot says nothing of them.

shaar_tadi.resume: The gate of the north, “which served no purpose.” According to R. Eliezer ben Yaakov (Middot 1:9), it was nonetheless through it that the kohen who became impure during the night went out. It is also the only gate in the whole Temple whose head is not a lintel: instead of a shkufa laid across it, two stones leaning against each other rest at the top and leave a triangle open. The Mishna counts it among the five gates of the Har HaBayit (Middot 1:3), and notes this exception in Middot 2:3.

10 × 20 amot; its slope and its span at the top are the tour's choice
